iterations.theme: What Every Woman Needs to Know Before Childbirth: Approach to Labor, Support for Mothers, and Personal Balance

sections.subtitle: From a Childhood in On-Call Shifts to Leading a Family Vocation
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik talks with host Ana Radišić in the pleasant ambiance of the hospital
sections.content:
In a new episode of the podcast, host **Ana Radišić** visited **Specijalna bolnica Podobnik**, a place where new lives come into the world every day. Her guest, gynecologist **dr. Petra Podobnik**, points out how unusual it feels for her to sit in hospital spaces in civilian clothes instead of a doctor's coat, given that the hospital is a place where she spends most of her daily life caring for mothers and newborns.

Although professionally deeply dedicated to medicine, dr. Podobnik emphasizes that motherhood brought her the greatest life transformation. As a mother of two children, she puts their well-being first, but also the importance of a healthy, supportive partner relationship and close friendships. Growing up alongside a mother neurologist who worked at **KBC Sestre milosrdnice (Vinogradska)** and a father gynecologist from **KB Merkur**, Petra Podobnik absorbed the medical way of life from an early age, spending time during their on-call shifts. Their unwavering dedication to patients also shaped her professional path. When her parents decided eighteen years ago to open a private hospital — in which more than seven thousand babies have been born so far — it was a logical continuation of the family vision of medicine as a true life vocation.

sections.subtitle: An Individual Approach to Pregnant Women and the Role of Psychotherapy in Medicine
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik explains the importance of psychological support and understanding patients
sections.content:
Commenting on work in the maternity ward, **dr. Petra Podobnik** points out that in her career she has welcomed hundreds and hundreds of babies, but emphasizes that the numbers do not matter. It is crucial to be fully present with each woman in labor. Recalling her work in the overburdened state system, she explained that for a doctor, a particular birth might be the tenth or twelfth in a shift, but for that woman it is the first or second in her life and it must remain a fond memory for her. It was precisely the desire to provide peace and individual dedication that was the foundation for creating a hospital environment in which pregnant women are monitored through multiple appointments before the birth itself in order to understand their fears and expectations.

In order to better understand patients, dr. Podobnik completed a five-year school of body-oriented psychotherapy. Although formally not a psychotherapist, the tools she acquired for her own development she applies daily in gynecological practice:

- Recognizing emotional blockages and fears in pregnant women
- Developing deep empathy without taking on someone else's burden
- Setting healthy professional boundaries to avoid burnout
- Open and clear communication when circumstances require a change in the medical plan

The doctor notes that experience has taught her to delegate tasks and accept the fact that outcomes cannot always be fully controlled.

sections.subtitle: Releasing Control: Facing the Fear of Childbirth
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik gestures while speaking about her own birth experience and letting go
sections.content:
Speaking about the fears pregnant women face, **dr. Petra Podobnik** states that pregnancy and childbirth are processes that are impossible to plan completely, despite modern diagnostics and ultrasound. She seeks to provide special care and a sense of security to women who arrive with traumas of previous pregnancy losses or difficult births, because restoring trust in one's own body and the medical team brings the greatest professional fulfillment.

Recalling her own experience of giving birth to a son fifteen years ago and a daughter ten years ago, the doctor admits that medical knowledge helped her realize only one thing — there is no planning. It was precisely complete surrender that led her to a quick and beautiful birth. Dr. Podobnik warns of a trend where women intensively prepare for months exclusively for the act of birth itself, creating fixed expectations that in practice often must adapt to the moment. Birth passes in a single day, whether it is a vaginal birth or a Caesarean section, and the real challenges begin the moment motherhood begins.

sections.subtitle: What a Baby Truly Needs in the First Year and Why Caring for the Mother Is a Priority
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Podobnik emphasizes the importance of supporting the mother after the child's arrival into the world
sections.content:
Debunking common myths of modern parenting, **dr. Petra Podobnik** emphasizes that a baby in the first year of life has basic needs: to be dry, fed, and in constant physical contact. She rejects the widespread belief that holding and carrying can "spoil a child in one's arms" and emphasizes that a baby seeks proximity that gives them a sense of security.

On the other hand, pressure from the environment and social media imposes unrealistic expectations on new mothers. While it was once taken for granted that "a whole village raises a child" and the baby was always in someone's arms, the Western world often forces premature independence and separation into a separate room. In the period of hormonal drops and the so-called *baby blues*, mothers often feel overburdened and lonely. Because of this, dr. Podobnik emphasizes a key premise: **caring for the mother is primary care for the baby**. If the mother is supported, rested, and emotionally stable, the child will also be well, which is why the support of a partner and immediate family in the first months is of crucial importance.

sections.subtitle: Personal Growth, More Humane Childbirth, and Finding Inner Peace
sections.screenshot_description: The guest speaks about a humane approach to giving birth and creating an intimate family space
sections.content:
Speaking candidly about her own beginnings in motherhood, **dr. Petra Podobnik** admits that in the beginning she was torn between work and new responsibilities. The turning point in her approach occurred when she became acquainted with the teachings of **Tomislav Kuljiš** at the **Centar za prirodno roditeljstvo (IPD centar)**. Through understanding the physiological needs of the child and working on her own internal patterns, she realized that a child's crying is not a problem in itself, but a signal that a parent must learn to accept calmly.

Speaking about the practice at **Specijalna bolnica Podobnik**, she emphasized the importance of humanizing childbirth — enabling intimacy, silence, and peace without unnecessary interference, where the family has the space for uninterrupted bonding with the newborn. For dr. Podobnik, medicine is a lifelong lesson in patience, compassion, and trust in life. When asked by host **Ana Radišić** how she recharges her own batteries, the doctor replies that it is simple things:

- Spending time in nature and trips to **Gorski kotar**, the homeland of her grandparents
- Walks with her dog and regular workouts
- Quality time spent with her children and close people
- Complete presence in the moment, whether in the operating room or in private life
